doc.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995

chapter: Drumming concepts and jazz as a word
title: The drummer as timekeeper and the bass drum with the bass
summary: The drummer's role is time; bass drum and bass fiddle worked as a team, it took seven years to control, and young drummers play solos but not time. Rhythm sections used to rehearse for dancers.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You know tell us about your concept of what the drummer does in the ensemble. What role does the drummer bring to jazz music?

Well to me, the drummer’s role, he is timekeeper. It’s not the bass player or the piano player, the drummer. The drummer is the basic in jazz. He is the basic man in jazz. But what has happened, it’s not easy playing bass drum. That’s why if you hear the different bands and things, everything is top, everything is on top. You don’t hear nothing at the bottom. There’s no bottom other than the bass. But when I was coming up, the drum and the bass player worked together as a team. This bass drum and the bass fiddle coincide with each other. And the bass drum was playing where he didn’t overpower the bass. It was felt, not heard, it was felt. And you don’t learn that overnight, I mean, being a drummer. See that’s another thing. You have to pay your dues. I mean it took me seven years to learn how to control the bass drum that I’d over play it or, and I’d keep time. Seven years. And if you was to feel this it’s nothing but muscle you know? Because of all those years of doing this. But that’s not easy. It’s not easy to do this and keep it steady, keep it going. And you start a tempo and you end up at that tempo. You don’t start under © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-

or over, you start at that tempo. But that takes years of experience. But today I mean the young drummers, you know I mean they’re learning all the rudiments. Yeah they all can play some of the greatest solos that you want to hear. I mean they frighten me with the solos that they play, because they know the rudiments and things. But when they’re supposed to do the job that they’re supposed to be doing, they don’t do it. They’re all over the drums. They’re not just playing [scats] playing the time, keeping the swinging.
Keeping the band swinging. I mean that’s an art in itself, isn’t it?

Yes. Well look I take great pride, in fact I play solos now because I have to because people want you to play solos. But I mean when I was coming up, I mean we took pride in how we swung the band, how we made the people dance. ‘Cause the music actually was created for dancing. It wasn’t created to sit and listen to. See that’s one of the things that I object to, that they’ve taken the music and, in a way, they’ve taken the rhythm out of it, for one thing, they’ve taken the rhythm — there’s no more rhythm section. We used to have a rhythm section rehearsal, just like the saxophone section rehearsed and the trumpet section and the trombone. The rhythm section had rehearsal. We’d have an arrangement and we’d say well we’ll play two beats here and we’ll play four beats here, and we’ll go into four here, and that. And that’s why those records sound the way that they do, those old records. Because there was a rhythm section there, which doesn’t happen today. The guy that’s playing the rhythm is the bass player. He’s got the whole load on himself. Now everybody else is doing, you know, what they do, doing their thing, yeah.
